Lessons.Title: Make Sense of Decimal Subtraction
ExplanationParagraphs: Original Grade5 Unit5 Lesson14 makes sense of subtraction to the hundredths and asks pupils to find their own justified method; place value, counting up and inverse addition are acceptable if correct.

Warm-up TRUE/FALSE source states 0.5−0.01=0.4 is FALSE, since difference 0.49; 0.61−0.02=0.59 is TRUE; 1−0.07=0.93 is TRUE. Ask why subtracting a HUNDREDTH changes the 0.5 hundredth position rather than dropping to0.4.

Activity1 The Difference original is 2.26−1.32=0.94. A place-value approach subtracts1 from2, 0.3 from0.2 requires regrouping, or counting up from1.32 to2.26 via1.32→2.00 (+0.68)→2.26 (+0.26), total0.94. The original learner method and explanation are TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED.

Activity2 Target Numbers original is the six-round partner game START AT2 and subtract the rolled number of TENTHS or HUNDREDTHS on each turn, seeking closest to1 WITHOUT GOING BELOW. No original sequence of rolls, no single preordained winner. Ask the learner to justify a different possible move.

Previous 94/36 shaded hundredths and 4.12−1.68 are mathematically correct but are first-party EXTENSIONS, never described as original source expressions. Original publisher Cool-down is gated; independently authored teacher Cool-down is separate.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: subtract decimals through hundredths using a student-chosen strategy, with a hundredths-grid visual or place-value argument, BEFORE treating the standard algorithm as obligatory. The 2021 source uses student mathematical posters and a Target Numbers game that starts from TWO instead of zero.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: describe a complete unit grid with 94 of 100 small squares shaded, then remove 36 of those hundredths. Explain the remaining 58 shaded hundredths using a diagram or inverse addition; all cells refer to the same original whole.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — show a subtraction method: 4.12−1.68=2.44. A counting-up explanation goes from 1.68 to 2.00 (+0.32), to 4.00 (+2.00), and to 4.12 (+0.12), totaling 2.44. A place-value method first subtracts one whole and regrouped fractional units; compare methods through first-party drawings or verbal representations. The student must explain why a comparison with a whole-number benchmark supports the result.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — Target Numbers subtraction: start at exactly 2.00 and use six provided digit-card values 4,2,3,1,2,1, each chosen ONCE as tenths or hundredths, to make a running total as close to 1 as possible without falling below 1. A legal example subtracts 0.4,0.2,0.3,0.01,0.02,0.01 for a final 1.06. Explain why the six choices fit the lower bound and propose how changing a digit from tenths to hundredths alters the result; this example is not claimed globally optimal.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: source goal includes creating and discussing visual subtraction displays, writing the six-step game record, refining choices and asking mathematical questions. Numeric 2.44 or 1.06 alone is not source-task completion; open representations, legality of decisions and communication require teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: Subtract with equal place units
KeyConcepts.Definition: Remove parts by matching hundredths to hundredths and tenths to tenths from the same whole.
KeyConcepts.Example: A grid of hundredths permits a first-party picture-based explanation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Count up to find a difference
KeyConcepts.Definition: Subtracting a from b is equivalent to the amount added to a to reach b.

KeyConcepts.Title: Game lower-bound objective
KeyConcepts.Definition: A six-choice subtraction record must stay at or above one and finish as close to one as possible.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Start 2.00, subtract assigned digits as tenths or hundredths; final ≥1.
KeyConcepts.Example: Comparing legal final results requires checking all stated choices and strategy.

WorkedExamples.Method: Original whole/tenths/hundredths subtraction with inverse-addition check; drawings and partner explanations remain teacher-judged.

Record all six choices in order and compare final number with one.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 1.06, so the example remains above one.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat 0.32 needed to reach 2 as an extra term to subtract again
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Counting-up increments already measure the difference and should be ADDED together once.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Record each incremental jump without overlapping intervals.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Give a numeric game result without six legal choices
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source also assesses place-value decisions and reflection after all six rolls.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Verify the complete record, legality, lower bound and explanation with a teacher.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat invented4.12−1.68 or 94/36 grid as the PRINTED lesson's main source tasks
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original IM2021 printed student activities use specific decimal values and require place-value reasoning, so substituting unrelated examples or accepting a right-justified digit alignment does not preserve source parity.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Restore actual source T/F and2.26−1.32, and preserve game outcomes as open teacher assessment.

SummaryPoints: Game requires six learner-specific rolls, subtraction of tenths or hundredths and nearest1 from above.
Optional prior: Decimal subtraction can be understood by removing equal-area hundredths, counting up or decomposing units.
Optional prior: Target Numbers Stage 9 starts at two and seeks one without dropping below it.
Optional prior: Drawing, game choices and justification are teacher-reviewed; arithmetic is a subcheck.

Lessons.Title: Estimate and Subtract
ExplanationParagraphs: Original Grade5 Unit5 Lesson15 estimates and subtracts decimal values, preserves place-value alignment including zero placeholders, and explains the written standard algorithm or a pupil-selected equivalent method.
Warm-up original Number Talk 1.50−0.51=0.99;1.50−0.52=0.98;1.50−0.60=0.90;1.50−0.62=0.88. Students explain shifts in the difference by hundredths and tenths.

Activity1 source 8.53−2.7=5.83 and6.62−3.71=2.91. Han's original vertical algorithm is embedded as an image; teacher verifies its actual composition steps and the learner's explanation rather than inventing pixel details.
Activity2 source 15.27−4.3=10.97, closest WHOLE11, and16.14−9.8=6.34, closest WHOLE6. Source requires estimated whole BEFORE exact subtraction, so assess both steps.

Optional Activity3 original622.35−71.4=550.95. Elena's erroneous right-aligned subtraction reports615.21 and Andre correctly aligns71.40 to get550.95. Benchmark620−70≈550 refutes Elena. Teacher assesses explicit correction of decimal-point columns.
Earlier correct fictional9.04−3.58,16.23−5.7,18.06−9.8 remain optional extensions, not source. Independently authored Edulytiks teacher Cool-down is distinct from original gated source.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: estimate decimal differences and use the subtraction standard algorithm while explaining HOW a larger place-value unit is decomposed into ten smaller units. The 2021 teacher/student activities contrast a chosen approach with algorithm steps, demand peer explanation revision, and include an optional critique of a right-alignment error.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: compare two whole-number benchmarks for 9.04−3.58. Because 9.04 is just above 9 and 3.58 is a little below 4, a reasonable difference estimate is a little above 5; more exact reasoning gives 5.46. The estimate is a magnitude check, not an artificial exact answer.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — make sense of decomposition: calculate 9.04−3.58 by writing 9.04−3.00−0.58 or by a correctly aligned standard algorithm. Regroup one tenth from the original nine whole units to create ten tenths, then one of those tenths to make ten hundredths for 4 hundredths −8 hundredths; explain the full exchange and verify result 5.46 through addition. A diagram and the explanation are assessed separately from the number.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — mixed precision and estimate: calculate 16.23−5.7 by writing 5.70, which gives 10.53, about 11. Calculate 18.06−9.8 as 18.06−10+0.2=8.26, about 8. Compare at least two valid strategies and state why decimal points must align rather than the rightmost printed digits.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Optional critique: a learner who writes 412.63−58.4 as 406.79 has effectively treated 58.4 as 5.84 through digit right-alignment. Use benchmark 410−60≈350 and 412.63−58.40=354.23 to reject 406.79, identify the misplaced digits and revise the explanation. This critique, alternative algorithms and teacher dialogue remain human-judged.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Assessment: source student response and secured Cool-down remain inaccessible. A checked numerical subtraction/estimate is a partial outcome; aligned columns, decomposed units, correct critique and documented teacher-reviewed explanations are required for original-task parity.

KeyConcepts.Title: Regroup tenths and hundredths during subtraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: When smaller-place digits cannot be subtracted, exchange one larger unit for ten of the next smaller unit without changing value.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 9.04−3.58=5.46, requiring regrouping in both tenths and hundredths.
KeyConcepts.Example: Nine wholes can exchange one whole into ten tenths, then one tenth into ten hundredths.

KeyConcepts.Title: Align decimal-place columns
KeyConcepts.Definition: A missing hundredths place in one number is zero, not a reason to shift the other number.
KeyConcepts.Example: The decimal point marks the alignment of equal units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compensation and estimation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Subtracting a nearby whole and compensating can simplify mixed-precision differences.
KeyConcepts.Example: Rounding predicts a magnitude, not a substitute for exact computation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Explain decomposing
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 9.04−3.58 with a correct place-value algorithm.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original whole/tenths/hundredths subtraction with inverse-addition check; drawings and partner explanations remain teacher-judged.
Steps: Write 9.04 and 3.58 in aligned columns.
Exchange one whole into ten tenths and one tenth into ten hundredths so 14 hundredths−8 hundredths is six and 9 tenths−5 tenths is four.
Subtract the three whole units from the eight remaining whole units, yielding five wholes.

WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate 16.23−5.7 and choose the nearest whole number.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original whole/tenths/hundredths subtraction with inverse-addition check; drawings and partner explanations remain teacher-judged.
Steps: Use 16−6≈10 as a rough estimate; refine after subtraction.
Write 5.7 as 5.70 and subtract by aligned place.
Compare 10.53 to neighboring integers 10 and 11.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Compensate for a near-ten subtrahend
WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate 18.06−9.8 efficiently.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original whole/tenths/hundredths subtraction with inverse-addition check; drawings and partner explanations remain teacher-judged.
Steps: Subtract ten first: 18.06−10=8.06.
Since 9.8 is 0.2 less than ten, add back 0.2.
Check the decimal place and compare to a rough 18−10 estimate.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Diagnose a right-alignment error
WorkedExamples.Question: A learner claims 412.63−58.4=406.79. Explain why that is invalid.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original whole/tenths/hundredths subtraction with inverse-addition check; drawings and partner explanations remain teacher-judged.
Steps: Estimate the correct result near 410−60≈350.
Notice the incorrect work effectively uses 5.84 instead of 58.4.
Align 58.40 under 412.63 and subtract correctly.
WorkedExamples.Check: 354.23+58.40=412.63; teacher reviews the specific alignment critique.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Subtract decimal digits that occupy different place values
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A wrong alignment changes the numeric size of the amount removed.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Pad with trailing zeros and align the decimal marks.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Forget to reduce a larger unit after exchanging it into ten smaller units
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Regrouping preserves total value by trading one for ten, not creating free additional units.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep a place-value exchange record and verify with inverse addition.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Right-align decimal last digits as if adding whole numbers, accepting Elena's615.21
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original IM2021 printed student activities use specific decimal values and require place-value reasoning, so substituting unrelated examples or accepting a right-justified digit alignment does not preserve source parity.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Align identical decimal places; verify622.35−71.40=550.95, and keep original source values.

SummaryPoints: Optional original622.35−71.40=550.95, Andre correct, Elena incorrect.
Optional prior: Estimate before computing and use the estimate to challenge implausible results.
Optional prior: Subtraction with decimals decomposes units when a place is too small.
Optional prior: The original peer discussion and optional algorithm critique require teacher adjudication.
